item.title: Protecting bosonic codes from ancilla-induced errors with continuous-variable flags
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Dispersively coupling an auxiliary harmonic oscillator mode (continuous-variable flag) to the control ancilla maps continuous ancilla-decay errors into phase-space displacements; heterodyne readout and feedback reduce cat-code parity measurement logical errors by more than three orders of magnitude.

Grade 0.468 · 2.4σ above the day's baseline · matched “photonic qubits, linear-optical computing and boson sampling” · Thomas Décultot, Ronan Gautier, Mazyar Mirrahimi

Figure

Logical error rate of four-component cat-code parity measurement as a function of flag amplitude or heterodyne measurement efficiency, showing over three orders of magnitude error reduction compared to the bare unflagged gate.

Asks

How can continuous errors propagated to a bosonic storage mode by ancilla decay during conditional gates be detected and corrected?

But

Simulations assume realistic circuit-QED parameters; one-flag conditional displacement protocol fails at first order when ancilla excitation occurs, requiring two flags to resolve arbitrary jump histories.

Tools

Continuous-variable flag mode · Dispersive qubit-oscillator coupling · Heterodyne detection and feedback · Echoed conditional displacement (ECD)

Abstract

Bosonic quantum error correction represents a route towards significant hardware overhead reduction for fault-tolerant quantum computation. However, controlling quantum harmonic oscillators that encode the quantum information comes with its own challenges. In many platforms such as superconducting circuits and trapped ions, the bosonic degree of freedom is controlled by an ancillary qubit whose decay during a qubit-oscillator gate propagates to the oscillator as a continuous error. Such errors generally lie beyond the scope of errors that the bosonic code is capable of correcting. We introduce the continuous-variable flag: an auxiliary oscillator coupled to the ancilla whose phase-space position encodes the continuous error corrupting the storage mode. After the gate, a heterodyne measurement of the flag estimates this continuous-variable error and a subsequent feedback control undoes it up to a bosonic code stabilizer. The scheme requires no new ingredients, as the flag is driven by the same dispersive coupling, displacements and rotations that implement the gates it is supposed to protect. We construct sequences protecting conditional rotations to all orders in ancilla decay with one flag, and conditional displacements to first order with one flag and to all orders with two. Simulations with realistic circuit-QED parameters predict more than three orders of magnitude fewer logical errors for the parity measurement of a four-component cat code, and a finite-energy GKP logical lifetime near its noiseless-ancilla bound. By discretizing continuous-variable errors, the flags introduced in this work are a useful tool for any hybrid oscillator-qubit processor, and open the route towards fault-tolerant simulation and computation with bosonic modes.

item.title: Excitation of subradiant states in atom chains by surface plasmon waves
item.description:
Pay dirt theory — Selective excitation of subradiant states with k>k0 in an atomic chain via propagating surface plasmon evanescent wave matching the subradiant mode wavenumber.

Grade 0.467 · 2.4σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum information with Rydberg atoms” · Giorgio Vimercati, Nicola Piovella

Figure

Momentum-space excitation distribution under surface plasmon driving versus direct laser driving. Surface plasmon driving selectively populates a subradiant mode beyond the light line at k=kx>k0.

Asks

How to selectively excite and prepare single subradiant collective modes beyond the light line in finite atomic chains?

But

Single-excitation regime ⟨σjz⟩≈−1. Neglects quantum correlations. Atomic chain parallel to flat metal surface.

Tools

coupled-dipole model · dyadic Green's tensor · Kretschmann configuration · Lorentz-Drude metal model

Abstract

Subradiant states of a finite subwavelength atomic chain in free space offer a powerful resource for photon storage. Yet their preparation and control remain challenging experimentally. A standard technique is to drive the atoms by a laser and observe the florescence light of the long-lived subradiant modes of excitation after the laser is switched off. However, these modes are highly degenerate and form an almost continuous band in the subradiant manifold. Here we propose a new method of exciting a given subradiant state by coupling atoms to a surface plasmon wave propagating along the interface with a metallic film. By controlling the chain/surface distance we may load, store and release photons in the atoms, making them a promising tool for future quantum memories.

item.title: Neural Correlation Learning for Quantum-Enhanced Sensing with Time-Independently Driven Rydberg Atom Arrays
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Evolving product states under unengineered time-independent Rydberg Hamiltonian dynamics achieves quantum-enhanced sensing surpassing the standard quantum limit, saturating the Cramér-Rao bound when decoded with a calibrated neural network.

Grade 0.423 · 1.8σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum information with Rydberg atoms” · Tao Zhang, Xiaotian Nie, Linghui Chen

Figure

Parameter posterior and estimation precision under incomplete calibration data. Top panel plots detuning posterior for an unseen pattern; bottom plots mean squared error and bias versus masked pattern fraction.

Asks

How can quantum-enhanced sensing sensitivity be extracted from complex many-body spatial correlations generated by native time-independent Hamiltonian dynamics without engineered entangled probe states?

Before

Coarse-grained collective readouts such as total Rydberg excitation number discard complex spatial correlations and lose the encoded metrological gain.

But

Numerical simulations restricted up to 3×3 (9 atoms) arrays; assumes time-independent homogeneous driving and local parameter estimation over discretized detuning bins.

Tools

Rydberg atom arrays · exact diagonalization · feedforward neural network decoder · Bayesian parameter inference · classical Fisher information

Code. https://github.com/ZhangTao1999/Neural_Correlation_Sensing_Code_Data

Abstract

Quantum-enhanced sensing typically relies on preparing specific entangled states. However, engineering these states in scalable many-body systems remains challenging due to the difficulty of designing robust preparation protocols and accounting for realistic noise. We show that evolving a simple product state under native time-independent Hamiltonian dynamics in Rydberg atom arrays generates complex many-body correlations that can potentially enable quantum-enhanced parameter estimation reaching the Heisenberg limit (HL). The key challenge is then shifted to extracting the metrological information encoded in spatial correlations of measurement patterns. We introduce a neural correlation learning framework that combines Bayesian inference with neural networks trained on calibration data. Operating in a two-stage calibration-and-sensing protocol, we numerically demonstrate that this framework effectively extracts many-body correlations to saturate the Cramér--Rao bound dictated by the classical Fisher information. Consequently, it achieves quantum-enhanced sensitivity surpassing the standard quantum limit (SQL). Furthermore, the learned estimator is robust to realistic noise, and remains accurate in the absence of rare measurement patterns. Our results establish a hardware-efficient and scalable paradigm for quantum sensing in interacting many-body systems without requiring engineered entangled states.

item.title: Sparse qubit operation in a 6×6 quantum dot array
item.description:
Worth a look new result — Operated 10 hole spin qubits simultaneously in a 6×6 quantum dot array with a shared barrier grid. Reduced crosstalk by 42× via sparse layout and demonstrated coherent spin shuttling across distances up to 5.2SIUnitSymbolMicro.

Grade 0.410 · 1.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “trapped-ion gates, shuttling and QCCD architectures” · Alexader S. Ivlev, Harold L. Co, Damien R. Crielaard, Alice Petrillo, Setareh Kazemzadeh, Giordano Scappucci, Menno Veldhorst

Figure

False-colour AFM image of the 6x6 quantum dot array with labelled plunger gates and merged barrier, alongside 2D maps of Spin Evolution Diagrams, g-factor, and coherence times extracted across the array.

Asks

Can extended 2D quantum dot arrays be operated with high-fidelity single- and two-qubit control without a dense wiring bottleneck?

But

30 of 36 dots coherently accessible; fixed global barrier gate voltage; two-qubit CZ fidelities limited to 66.8±6.0%--71.5±2.5% by dephasing and slow shuttling.

Tools

merged-barrier 6x6 quantum dot array · Ge/SiGe heterostructure · bucket-brigade spin shuttling · Spin Evolution Diagrams · EDSR

Abstract

Fault-tolerant quantum computation requires increasing the qubit count while maintaining high performance and connectivity. Semiconductor qubits have demonstrated high-fidelity operation, but growing the system size at sufficient connectivity remains challenging, such that scaling mainly occurred in one spatial direction to preserve access for control lines in the other. Here, we realise an approach that relaxes the requirements on fabrication and demonstrate a 6×6 quantum dot array, defined by a shared barrier gate and individual plunger gates. The quantum dots are tuned through coherent spin shuttling over distances up to 5.2um into a sparse configuration of 10 simultaneously operated qubits, leaving space for shuttling connections. We reduce crosstalk by 42× in this separated regime, enabling high-fidelity simultaneous single-qubit control, while control-Z operations can be implemented through shuttling and plunger-only control. These results promise high-connectivity quantum circuits, enabled by scaling to two-dimensional geometries and exploiting shuttling.
